overview.title: Choosing how to annotate, and the danger of nonrepresentative data
overview.chapter: 6 The universal workflow of machine learning
overview.main_topic: Trade-offs in annotation sourcing and tooling; requirement that training data be representative of production data
overview.central_idea: Choose an annotation strategy by weighing control, cost, noise and the expertise the labels require, and invest early in annotation software. Above all, training data must be representative of production data. A model with over 90% test accuracy can be wrong 8 times out of 10 in deployment if it was trained on the wrong kind of data.
overview.importance: Nonrepresentative data is one of the most common and costly failures in applied ML because test-set metrics do not reveal it. This page says representativeness should be 'the foundation of all of your data collection work.'
learning_objectives: Weigh outsourcing (cheap, scalable, noisy, less control) against in-house annotation.
Use the three constraint questions (expertise needed, trainability of labelers, your own understanding of the labels) to pick an annotation strategy.
Explain why annotation software deserves early investment.
Define representative training data and explain how the dish-photo app failed despite a high test accuracy.
State the book's remedy: collect data from the production environment, or understand and actively correct train/production differences.
Recognize concept drift as a related phenomenon (defined on p.201).
prerequisites: Annotation options listed on p.199 (self, crowdsourcing, labeling company).

summary:
The page continues **Investing in data annotation infrastructure** from p.199. **Outsourcing** can save time and money but *takes away control*. **Mechanical Turk** is likely inexpensive and scales well, but annotations may be *quite noisy*.

To choose, the book asks you to consider three constraints:

- **Do labelers need to be subject matter experts?** Anyone can label cat vs. dog, dog breeds need specialized knowledge, and annotating **CT scans of bone fractures** "pretty much requires a medical degree."
- **If expertise is needed, can you train people?** If not, how will you reach the experts?
- **Do you yourself understand how experts annotate?** If not, the dataset is a **black box** and you cannot do manual feature engineering. This "isn't critical, but it can be limiting."

If you label **in-house**, decide what software will record annotations. You may have to build it, and *productive annotation software* is worth investing in early.

The next subsection, **Beware of nonrepresentative data**, states the main principle: models only make sense of inputs similar to what they have seen, so training data must be **representative of production data**. This should be "the foundation of all of your data collection work."

The example is a dish-recognition app trained on polished photos from a foodie social network. Test accuracy is **well over 90%**, but in production it is **wrong 8 times out of 10**. Users' casual phone photos look nothing like the training images. The authors call this "a cardinal sin—welcome to machine learning hell."

The remedy is to **collect data directly from the deployment environment**. An IMDB sentiment model should run on new IMDB reviews, not Yelp reviews or tweets. To score tweets, annotate real tweets from similar users. If that is impossible, *fully understand how training and production data differ and actively correct for it*. The page ends by introducing **concept drift**, which is defined on p.201.

paragraphs.what_it_says: Outsourcing annotation can save time and money but reduces your control. Mechanical Turk is probably cheap and scalable, but its annotations can be quite noisy.
paragraphs.what_it_means: There is a three-way trade-off between cost/scale, label quality and control over the process. Crowdsourcing is strong on the first and weak on the other two.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: Since target quality determines model quality (p.199), cheap noisy labels can cost more in the end than they save.
paragraphs.technical_idea: Beyond the book: crowd label noise is often reduced by collecting several labels per item and aggregating them (majority vote or annotator-reliability models), plus 'gold' check items.

terminology.meaning: Labels that are frequently wrong or inconsistent across annotators.
Having people outside your team (crowd or vendor) produce labels.

connections: p.199: the three annotation options are introduced.

paragraphs.excerpt: Do the data labelers need to be subject matter experts, or could anyone
paragraphs.what_it_says: First constraint: do labelers need to be experts? Cat vs. dog can be labeled by anyone, dog breeds require specialized knowledge, and CT scans of bone fractures pretty much require a medical degree.
paragraphs.what_it_means: The three examples form a scale of required expertise, and the right sourcing option depends on where your task falls. Crowdsourcing works at the low end and fails at the high end.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: Labels from people without the needed expertise are noise, not signal.

terminology.meaning: A person with the domain knowledge needed to assign correct labels.

connections: p.199: cookie labelers can be trained, while satellite labels need archaeologists.

paragraphs.excerpt: If annotating the data requires specialized knowledge, can you train people to do
paragraphs.what_it_says: Second constraint: if expertise is needed, can you train people to provide it? If not, how do you get access to experts?
paragraphs.what_it_means: Some expertise can be taught in a short training, such as spotting bad cookies (p.199). Other expertise, like radiology, cannot, and expert time becomes the bottleneck.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: This often decides how quickly and cheaply you can scale annotation.
connections: p.199: 'you should be able to train people to do it' (cookie project).

paragraphs.excerpt: Do you, yourself, understand the way experts come up with the annotations? If
paragraphs.what_it_says: Third constraint: do you understand how experts arrive at their labels? If not, you must treat the dataset as a black box and cannot do manual feature engineering. That is not critical but can be limiting.
paragraphs.what_it_means: Understanding the labeling logic lets you design features, check labels and debug the model. Without it, you rely entirely on the model to find the signal.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: It links to p.202's warning that treating a dataset as a black box is bad practice, and to the feature-engineering discussion in chapter 5.

terminology.meaning: Hand-designing input representations that make the target easier to learn.
Data whose meaning and labeling logic you don't understand.

connections: p.202: 'It's bad practice to treat a dataset as a black box.'

paragraphs.excerpt: If you decide to label your data in-house, ask yourself what software you
paragraphs.what_it_says: For in-house labeling, decide what software will record annotations. You may need to build it. Productive annotation software saves a lot of time and is worth investing in early.
paragraphs.what_it_means: Annotation throughput depends heavily on tooling: keyboard shortcuts, pre-filled suggestions, quick review. Over hundreds of thousands of items, small per-item savings add up.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: It treats annotation as infrastructure, in line with the subsection title.

terminology.meaning: A tool that shows samples to labelers and records their labels.

connections: p.213: keep collecting and annotating data and keep improving your annotation pipeline after deployment.

paragraphs.excerpt: Machine learning models can only make sense of inputs that are similar to
paragraphs.what_it_says: Models only make sense of inputs similar to what they have seen, so training data must be representative of production data. This should be the foundation of all data collection work.
paragraphs.what_it_means: This follows from generalization by interpolation. A model is reliable only within the region of input space its training data covers. Production inputs outside that region are extrapolation.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: The book places this concern above every other data-collection consideration.
paragraphs.technical_idea: Beyond the book: in standard terminology this is the requirement that training and production data come from the same distribution, and its violation is called distribution shift (covariate shift when the input distribution changes).

terminology.meaning: Training data drawn from the same kind of inputs, conditions and users the model will face in production.
The inputs the deployed model actually receives.

connections: p.183: generalization originates from the latent structure and dense sampling of the data.

paragraphs.excerpt: Suppose you’re developing an app where users can take pictures of a dish
paragraphs.what_it_says: A dish-recognition app trained on photos from a foodie social network scores well over 90% on its test set but is wrong 8 times out of 10 after deployment. Users' phone photos of random dishes from random restaurants look nothing like the professional, well-lit training images. The training data wasn't representative of production data, which the book calls a cardinal sin.
paragraphs.what_it_means: The test set came from the same unrepresentative source as the training set, so it could not reveal the problem. A high test score only means the model works on data like the test set.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: This is why you should evaluate on data that looks like production data, and why monitoring after deployment (p.212) is needed.
paragraphs.technical_idea: The accuracy drop goes from >90% to about 20% (2 right out of 10). Test accuracy estimates performance on the test distribution, not on the production distribution.

terminology.meaning: The authors' phrase for the most serious mistake in data collection.

connections: p.212: monitoring the model in the wild and manual audits of production predictions.

paragraphs.excerpt: If possible, collect data directly from the environment where your model will be
paragraphs.what_it_says: If possible, collect data from the environment where the model will be used. An IMDB sentiment model should be applied to new IMDB reviews, not Yelp reviews or tweets. To rate tweets, collect and annotate real tweets from users similar to those expected in production. If you cannot train on production data, fully understand the differences and actively correct them.
paragraphs.what_it_means: Representativeness includes the source, the style of text or image, and the user population. Even within one medium such as text, a change of platform changes vocabulary, length and tone.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: It gives a clear order of preference: production data first, and otherwise a documented, corrected proxy.

terminology.meaning: Beyond the book: training and deployment data coming from different sources or styles.

connections: IMDB sentiment classification is the binary-classification example from chapter 4.

paragraphs.excerpt: A related phenomenon you should be aware of is concept drift. You’ll encounter
paragraphs.what_it_says: The book introduces concept drift, which you will meet in almost all real-world problems, especially those involving user-generated data (the sentence continues on p.201).
paragraphs.what_it_means: Nonrepresentativeness can develop over time even when training data starts out representative, because production data changes.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: It sets up p.201's definition: production data properties change over time and accuracy gradually decays.

terminology.meaning: Change in the properties of production data over time that degrades a trained model (defined on p.201).

connections: p.201: definition and examples of concept drift (2013 music recommender, 2011 IMDB data, fraud).

concepts.name: Data annotation
concepts.definition: Producing targets for inputs; the sourcing choice trades off cost, scale, control and label noise.
concepts.intuition: Cheap labels can be expensive if they are wrong.
concepts.technical: Constraints: required expertise, trainability of labelers, your own understanding of the labeling logic, and tooling.
concepts.example: Cat vs. dog (anyone), dog breeds (specialists), bone-fracture CT scans (medical degree).
concepts.misconception: Crowdsourcing works for any labeling task; it fails when labels need expertise.

concepts.name: Crowdsourced labeling
concepts.definition: Labeling through platforms like Mechanical Turk: inexpensive and scalable but potentially quite noisy.
concepts.intuition: Fast and cheap, but you give up control over quality.
concepts.technical: Beyond the book: noise is mitigated with redundancy and agreement-based aggregation.
concepts.significance: A good fit for tasks anyone can label.
concepts.misconception: Scale makes up for noise; systematic noise does not average out.

concepts.name: Representative training data
concepts.definition: Training data similar to the data the model will see in production.
concepts.intuition: You can only recognize what you've seen before.
concepts.technical: Beyond the book: same-distribution assumption; violations are distribution shift.
concepts.significance: Called the foundation of all data collection work; violating it is 'a cardinal sin'.
concepts.example: Foodie-network dish photos vs. casual smartphone photos: >90% test accuracy, 8/10 wrong in production.
concepts.misconception: High test accuracy guarantees production performance; not if the test set shares the training set's bias.

concepts.name: Concept drift
concepts.definition: Change over time in production data properties that causes model accuracy to decay (full definition on p.201).
concepts.intuition: The world moves on while the model stays fixed.
concepts.technical: Requires ongoing data collection, annotation and retraining.
concepts.significance: Encountered in almost all real-world problems, especially with user-generated data.
concepts.misconception: Representative data at training time stays representative.

deeper.title: Why the test set didn't catch the dish-app problem
deeper.body:
1. The team scraped polished photos from a foodie network.
2. They split that data into train and test, so **both came from the same source**.
3. Test accuracy above 90% correctly measured performance on *foodie-network-style photos*.
4. Production inputs (dim, casual, random restaurants and phones) came from a different distribution.
5. Performance fell to about 20% correct.

Inference: the fix is not only better training data. Your **evaluation** data should also come from production conditions. Even a small hand-labeled sample of real user uploads would have shown the gap before launch.

deeper.title: A decision guide for annotation sourcing
deeper.body:
Built from the book's three questions (arrangement ours):

- *Anyone can label?* Crowdsourcing is viable; plan for noise.
- *Needs expertise, but trainable?* Train in-house labelers or use a labeling company; invest in tooling.
- *Needs scarce experts (e.g., radiologists)?* Arrange expert access; expert time is the bottleneck.
- *You don't understand the experts' logic?* Expect to treat the dataset as a black box; no manual feature engineering.

deeper.title: Representativeness as matching your customers
deeper.body: Training a chef only on photos from glossy cookbooks and then asking them to identify dishes from blurry phone pictures in a dim restaurant is unfair to the chef. The model is in the same position.

misconceptions.claim: If my test accuracy is above 90%, my app will work for users.
misconceptions.correction: Only if test data resembles production data. The dish app scored over 90% on its test set and was wrong 8 times out of 10 in production.

misconceptions.claim: Any text sentiment data will do for any sentiment task.
misconceptions.correction: The book says an IMDB model should be used on IMDB reviews, not Yelp reviews or tweets; collect data from the actual target environment and user population.

misconceptions.claim: Not understanding how experts label is a fatal problem.
misconceptions.correction: The book says it isn't critical but limiting: you must treat the data as a black box and can't do manual feature engineering.

earlier.note: Annotation options and the claim that annotation quality determines model quality.
Dataset curation and generalization from the data.

later.note: Concept drift defined; sampling bias (Dewey defeats Truman).
Understanding your data; not treating a dataset as a black box; target leaking.
Monitoring the deployed model and auditing production predictions.
Keep collecting and annotating data and improving the annotation pipeline.

takeaways: Outsourcing annotation saves time and money but takes away control; crowdsourcing is cheap and scalable but noisy.
Choose an annotation strategy by asking whether labelers need expertise, whether it can be taught, and whether you understand the experts' logic.
Invest early in productive annotation software if labeling in-house.
Training data must be representative of production data; this is the foundation of all data collection work.
A high test score on unrepresentative data says nothing about production: >90% test vs. 8/10 wrong in deployment.
Collect data from the real deployment environment and user population, or understand and actively correct the differences.

questions.question: According to the book, what is the main downside of using a platform like Mechanical Turk for labels?
options: Annotations may end up being quite noisy
questions.answer: Annotations may end up being quite noisy
questions.explanation: The book says Mechanical Turk is likely inexpensive and scales well, which rules out the first two options, but labels can be noisy. The medical degree refers to the CT-scan example.

questions.question: Give the book's three examples showing increasing labeling expertise.
questions.answer: Cat vs. dog (anyone), dog breed classification (specialized knowledge), CT scans of bone fractures (pretty much requires a medical degree).
questions.explanation: These appear in the first constraint bullet.

questions.question: The dish app had well over 90% test accuracy yet was wrong 8 out of 10 times in production. Why didn't the test set reveal the problem?
questions.answer: The test set came from the same unrepresentative source (polished foodie-network photos) as the training data, so it measured performance on that distribution, not on users' casual smartphone photos.
questions.explanation: Test accuracy only estimates performance on data distributed like the test set. The book states the root cause: the training data wasn't representative of the production data.

questions.question: You want to rate the sentiment of tweets. What does the book recommend?
options: Train on IMDB reviews since they are well labeled
Train on Yelp reviews, which are short like tweets
Collect and annotate actual tweets from a similar set of users as expected in production
Use any sentiment dataset and fine-tune later
questions.answer: Collect and annotate actual tweets from a similar set of users as expected in production
questions.explanation: The book's advice is to collect data from the environment where the model will be used. IMDB and Yelp data are different domains, and the last option ignores the representativeness requirement.

questions.question: What does the book say to do if you cannot train on production data?
questions.answer: Make sure you fully understand how your training and production data differ, and actively correct these differences.
questions.explanation: Stated at the end of the 'If possible, collect data directly…' paragraph.

questions.question: What do you lose if you don't understand how experts arrive at their annotations, and how serious is it according to the book?
questions.answer: You must treat the dataset as a black box and can't perform manual feature engineering. The book says this isn't critical but can be limiting.
questions.explanation: This is the third constraint bullet.

questions.question: For a model you have built or used, list three ways production inputs could differ from its training data (source, conditions, user population), and how you would check for each.
questions.answer: Answers vary; e.g., different camera quality, different user demographics, different time period, each checked by sampling and labeling real production data.
questions.explanation: This applies the page's representativeness principle to your own work.
